ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all UBOs, directors, officers, signatories, and material shareholders against the EU Consolidated Financial Sanctions List, the UN Security Council Consolidated List, the OFAC SDN List, national asset-freezing measures under Articles L562-1 et seq. of the French Monetary and Financial Code, and Tracfin guidance. Politically Exposed Persons are identified under FATF methodology and the French transposition of Directive (EU) 2015/849 and Directive (EU) 2018/843. Enhanced due diligence is mandatory for PEPs, high-risk third-country nationals, and structures involving offshore intermediaries or nominee arrangements. Screening is required at onboarding, immediately before filing, and then on a periodic basis of at least every 90 days.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Guichet Unique des Formalités des Entreprises via formalites.entreprises.gouv.fr (official digital filing portal administered by INPI); name availability verification additionally supported by the Registre National des Entreprises (RNE) and the Infogreffe RCS database (infogreffe.fr).
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Under Law No. 94-665 of 4 August 1994 (Loi Toubon), all official instruments, commercial correspondence, and public documents produced for filing in France must be in French. A corporate name may be formed using French or a foreign language expressed in Latin or romanized characters; non-Latin scripts such as Chinese characters are not accepted as the primary registered denomination. Chinese or other non-Latin names must be transliterated into a Latin form (e.g., Hanyu Pinyin) in the articles of association and may be added as a secondary alias on the company's letterhead, provided the French statutory information is also included. The legal form 'SAS' must appear in the corporate name and in all correspondence.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: A stand-alone name reservation is not issued by the French guichet unique; rather, the name is cleared at the point of filing and protected while the registration file is being processed. In practice, the availability check is treated as valid for 30 days. If the name is rejected, the applicant must file a new formation application with a distinctive alternative name. Against a formal refusal by the greffier, the applicant may submit a written challenge to the juge commis à la surveillance du registre within 15 days of the reasoned refusal; if that judge maintains the refusal, an appeal lies to the First President of the Cour d'appel within one month. There is no statutory extension of the 30-day clearance window, so a fresh Infogreffe availability search is required before re-filing.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permitted for an SAS engaged in information-technology consulting and offshore software development, provided the registered office is established through a licensed domiciliation company under Articles L123-11 to L123-11-4 of the French Commercial Code. The domiciliation contract must provide an actual address in France, physical handling of correspondence, and availability of documents for inspection. A purely virtual address without local substance may be challenged by the French tax and social authorities as an abuse of law, especially where the enterprise is presented as an offshore development center while lacking any local administrative, accounting, or personnel infrastructure.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Approximately 15% probability of an unannounced physical inspection within the first 24 months for a foreign-owned ODC using a virtual registered office. The probability rises to approximately 25% if the company files VAT returns, has no local employees, and shows no substantive decision-making presence in France. URSSAF, INSEE, and tax auditors may conduct on-site verification visits without prior notice.

incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: The undersigned subscriber and proposed manager resolve to incorporate the Company as a Société par Actions Simplifiée (SAS) under French law. The initial share capital is fixed at ONE EURO (1 EUR), represented by one share of the same amount, subscribed in full by the sole shareholder. The registered office is established at the address set forth below. [Full Name] is appointed sole Gérant (Manager) with full powers of administration and representation, including opening bank accounts, signing contracts, and filing all documents with the RCS. The Manager is authorized to execute the Acte de Création, publish the incorporation in the BALO, and take all steps necessary for incorporation and initial operations. This resolution is adopted unanimously.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Direction Générale des Finances Publiques (DGFiP) with business client portal at impots.gouv.fr; corporate and statutory identifier registration via the Guichet Unique des Formalités d'Entreprises (formalites.entreprises.gouv.fr) and the Greffe du Tribunal de Commerce (RCS); SIREN/SIRET assigned by INSEE; VAT registration issued by the DGFiP's Service des Impôts des Entreprises (SIE) under Article 286 ter of the French General Tax Code (Code Général des Impôts, CGI).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: 1) Incorporate the SAS through the Guichet Unique: file statutory documents (statuts, président designation, registered office proof) and obtain RCS registration (Kbis extract); 2) Upon RCS registration, receive the 9-digit SIREN national identifier and, with the first establishment, the 14-digit SIRET; 3) File VAT registration with the competent Service des Impôts des Entreprises using Form 3310-CA3 (French-established entity) or Form 3310-A (foreign entities); 4) DGFiP issues the TVA intracommunautaire number in the format FR + 2-digit key + SIREN; 5) If the SAS has a non-EU legal representative or is controlled by non-residents, no French fiscal representative is required so long as the SAS itself is established in France with effective management in France; 6) Register with the Portail Public de Facturation (PPF) or a certified Plateforme de Dématérialisation Partenaire (PDP) in advance of the e-invoicing deadlines; 7) Appoint a same-day or wire-enabled EUR bank account and, where invoices are settled in foreign currency, maintain an MT103/SWIFT or Wise/Payoneer settlement archive supporting FX conversion for VAT and corporate tax reconciliation.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation — the SAS is a French-resident limited company taxable on worldwide profits at the corporate income tax rate (Impôt sur les Sociétés, IS) under Article 209 CGI when the registered office or effective management is in France; the standard headline IS rate is 25% from fiscal years opened in 2022 onward, with the reduced 15% rate applicable to the first €42,500 of taxable profit for eligible small enterprises (turnover below €10M); the SAS is the direct tax taxpayer and has no pass-through classification in France; capital gains are included in ordinary corporate income at 25%; non-resident shareholders are not taxed at entity level, and the 30% flat tax (PFU) applies to distributed dividends subject to treaty relief and 25% withholding where applicable.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: 1) No check-the-box election exists in France: a SAS cannot be treated as a disregarded pass-through entity; 2) Election for French tax consolidation ('intégration fiscale', Article 223 A CGI) is available where the SAS owns at least 95% of French subsidiaries, filed with the DGFiP by the consolidating parent; 3) Election for the small-business VAT exemption waiver ('option sur la franchise en base', Article 293 D CGI) enables a qualifying SAS to submit periodic VAT returns despite being below the franchise thresholds; 4) Election for monthly VAT returns under the normal regime is available even when the simplified regime applies, allowing better claim timing for input VAT credits; 5) Hybrid mismatch election: France implements ATAD (EU Directive 2016/1164) via Articles 212-1 A to 212-1 H CGI; no domestic hybrid election is available, but the SAS must file relevant controlled-transaction disclosures with the DGFiP annual tax return (Form 2257-SD) and, if part of an MNE group above the thresholds, file the Country-by-Country Report, transfer pricing documentation, and Form 2258-SD.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: VAT — Taxe sur la Valeur Ajoutée (TVA), governed by Articles 256 to 289 quater CGI and the national transposition of Directive 2006/112/EC; administered by DGFiP with customs controls by the Direction Générale des Douanes et Droits Indirects (DGDDI); the reverse-charge and EU One-Stop-Shop (OSS) mechanisms apply fully.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: A French-established SAS must register for TVA from the first euro of taxable activity: there is no minimum turnover threshold for resident taxable persons; however, the 'franchise en base de TVA' exemption (Article 293 B CGI) applies to domestic-only sales below €91,900 (supplies of goods) and €36,800 (provision of services) per calendar year, with specific upward adjustment rules; since the ODC renders cross-border B2B services, mandatory registration applies regardless of turnover and the franchise is generally not exercised; for non-established foreign suppliers, the EU-OSS distance sales threshold is €10,000 EU-wide, which does not apply to this French-established SAS.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: France has adopted mandatory structured e-invoicing and e-reporting: issuance and receipt of electronic invoices must occur through certified dematerialization platforms (PDP) connected to the national Portail Public de Facturation (PPF) per Decree 2022-1299; new statutory calendar: from 1 September 2026, all taxable persons must receive e-invoices and large/mid-size enterprises must issue structured e-invoices and e-report cross-border transactions; from 1 September 2027, SMEs and micro-enterprises must issue structured e-invoices and e-report; invoices must comply with the EN 16931 semantic standard (Factur-X, UBL or CII); France does not operate real-time fiscal clearance or digital stamping (no continuous transaction controls) — instead, the PPF applies post-factum data exchange, DGFiP machine-audit, and matching of e-invoice datasets against VAT returns, recapitulative statements (DEB), and intrastat reports; taxpayers must retain full audit-supporting data for six years under Article L.102 B of the Livre des Procédures Fiscales (LPF).

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: The offshore software development services supplied by the SAS qualify for zero-rating / exclusion from French VAT as follows: (1) B2B services supplied to a taxable person established in another EU Member State are outside the scope of French VAT under Article 259-1 B CGI and Article 44 of Directive 2006/112/EC — the French supplier invoices at 0% French VAT with the mention 'autoliquidation / reverse charge' and reports the transaction in the DEB; (2) B2B services supplied to taxable persons established outside the EU are considered performed outside France unless one of the limited use-and-enjoyment exceptions in Article 259 B CGI applies (services physically performed in France, services relating to French real property or tangible property located in France) — none of these exceptions apply to dedicated offshore code development and software maintenance consumed abroad; generalized and abstract zero-rating for export requires proof that the recipient is a taxable person in its jurisdiction (valid VAT number via VIES for EU; certificate of corporate residence or VAT registration for third countries), a written contract describing deliverables and the outside-France use, and evidence of payment settlement from the non-resident customer; provision of services to French-resident establishments would remain taxable at 20% French VAT, so the ODC must maintain a clear 'place of supply' analysis and avoid relying solely on headquarters outside France.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (DAU) lodged in DELTA-X/DELTA-G with MRN where goods co-shipments (servers, dev kits) are present — Directive Générale des Douanes et Droits Indirects export clearance record
Signed ODC master services agreement with the non-resident customer specifying the place of establishment, deliverables, payment terms, and intellectual property transfer
Structured e-invoice (Factur-X / EN 16931) or PDF invoice carrying the explicit 0% VAT line and statutory mention 'TVA non applicable — article 259-1 B CGI' for EU supplies
Bill of Lading / airway bill evidencing physical dispatch from French territory for any bundled physical components
Inward Remittance Certificate, Swift MT103 wire credit advice, or Wise/Payoneer settlement report matching the invoiced EUR or FX-equivalent amount within commercial terms

Recapitulative statement (DEB / Déclaration d'Échanges de Services) filing receipt evidencing intra-Community zero-rated supplies filed monthly where the quarterly total exceeds €50,000 and quarterly otherwise, required by the 10th day of the month following the period
VIES customer VAT validation record and, for third-country customers, a certificate of tax residence or official local VAT/gst registration confirming non-establishment in France
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: DGFiP audits (vérification de comptabilité) apply intense scrutiny to export zero-rating and outside-scope claims: 1) Article 1729 CGI imposes a 40% penalty for intentional tax misstatement (manquement délibéré) and 80% penalty where fictitious documentation or sham cross-border invoicing is established (manœuvres frauduleuses); 2) Late-payment interest accrues at 0.20% per month (2.4% p.a.) on rectified VAT under Article 1727 CGI; 3) Omission from the DEB triggers a €15-per-transaction penalty capped at €250 under Article 1735 ter CGI, and non-compliant e-invoice data triggers a €15-per-invoice penalty capped at €15,000 annually under Article 1737 CGI; 4) Repeated false export claims may be recharacterized as criminal tax fraud (Article 1741 Code pénal) punishable by up to five years imprisonment and a €500,000 fine, with aggravated aggravated-scope up to seven years and €750,000; 5) The standard three-year statute of limitation under Article L.169 LPF extends to ten years where no return was filed or the activity was deliberately concealed; 6) EU cross-institutional checks (Eurofisc, VIES data matching) enable the DGFiP to identify mismatches between the French seller's 0% position and the customer's reverse-charge entries; if the customer omits the transaction, the DGFiP reasserts French VAT, derecognizes input VAT credits, and imposes retroactive assessments with penalties and interest; 7) The SAS must retain the full documentation bundle for six years (Article L.102 B LPF) and ensure transfer pricing of the offshore model supports arm's-length compensation so that recharacterization as a French taxable fixed establishment does not occur.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Banque de France is France’s central bank and part of the Eurosystem. The European Central Bank sets euro-area monetary policy. The French Treasury (Direction générale du Trésor) administers applicable foreign-investment controls; the Autorité de contrôle prudentiel et de résolution supervises relevant financial institutions. France applies EU and French law.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The euro is freely convertible, and France has no general exchange-control restrictions on ordinary current-account payments or capital movements. Cross-border transfers remain subject to sanctions, anti-money-laundering, tax, statistical-reporting, and, where applicable, foreign-investment rules. A French SAS may generally pay dividends and other lawful amounts abroad after corporate approval, availability of distributable profits, applicable withholding-tax analysis, and completion of bank checks. Interest, royalties, service fees, and related-party payments require substantiation and compliance with transfer-pricing, deductibility, and withholding-tax rules. An inbound investment may require French foreign-investment screening if the investor, activity, or transaction falls within the statutory regime; an ordinary software-development activity is not, by itself, a listed sensitive activity.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: France has no general statutory deadline requiring export proceeds to be repatriated to France and no mandatory conversion ratio for export receipts. Receipts may be retained in foreign currency, subject to contractual, tax, accounting, sanctions, and bank documentation requirements. Banks and companies may have statistical-reporting obligations for cross-border transactions under applicable Banque de France and EU reporting rules; these are not a general surrender or conversion requirement.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium to High for routine EUR and supported-currency collections and payments, subject to the provider’s country, activity, and risk acceptance. Use an electronic-money institution or payment institution authorized in France or passported under EU law. An EMI balance is electronic money safeguarded under applicable rules, not a bank deposit and generally not covered by deposit-guarantee schemes. Confirm that the provider accepts a French SAS, supports the required currencies and payment purposes, and permits capital transactions; do not assume an EMI can provide a legally acceptable capital-deposit certificate. Retain a conventional bank account for capital formalities, tax payments, and contingency liquidity.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: French law does not generally require directors to appear physically at a bank branch to open a corporate account. Remote onboarding may be available, but the bank sets its own identity-verification, original-document, certified-translation, video-interview, and signatory requirements. Non-resident directors, complex ownership chains, or higher-risk geographies may trigger an in-person interview or additional verification. A formation capital account must satisfy the bank’s documentary requirements before it issues the deposit certificate.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident ownership, layered holding companies, nominee arrangements, or difficulty identifying natural-person ultimate beneficial owners.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide a dated ownership chart through to natural-person beneficial owners; constitutional documents and registers for each intermediate entity; identity and address evidence for beneficial owners, directors, and authorized signatories; beneficial-ownership filings where applicable; and explanations for any ownership or control rights that are not apparent from the chart.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unclear source of capital, unusually large initial funding, third-party funding, or capital received from a jurisdiction inconsistent with the business profile.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide signed subscription and shareholder resolutions, incorporation or capital-increase documents, bank statements tracing funds to the investor, audited accounts or tax records supporting source of wealth, the investor’s corporate approvals, and a clear payment reference linking the transfer to the SAS capital transaction.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cross-border payments inconsistent with a software-development business, including unexplained cash activity, high-risk counterparties, crypto-related flows, or payments involving sanctioned jurisdictions or persons.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide customer and supplier contracts, invoices, statements of work, delivery evidence, counterparty identification, sanctions-screening records, a documented payments policy, and an explanation of the commercial purpose and expected volume, geography, and frequency of transactions. Reject or escalate prohibited or unresolved sanctions matches.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Material related-party service, royalty, interest, or management-fee payments without clear services, pricing support, or beneficial ownership information.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide intercompany agreements, invoices, deliverables or time records, functional and benefit analysis, transfer-pricing support, tax and withholding analysis, counterparty ownership information, and corporate approvals.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: For incorporation, arrange the subscriber’s transfer to a bank-approved capital-deposit account and provide the draft articles, proposed share-capital details, subscriber identity and ownership information, and source-of-funds evidence. The bank issues a deposit certificate after checks; release of funds follows registration and delivery of the required registration evidence. For a later capital increase, obtain the required shareholder or corporate approvals and follow the bank’s capital-deposit and release process. Route funds from an account in the investor’s own name where practicable, in the subscribed currency or EUR as agreed with the bank. Use a precise payment reference such as “share capital subscription” or “capital increase,” not a generic trade purpose. There is no universal French FX purpose-code requirement for ordinary capital transfers; provide the bank’s requested purpose, transaction documents, and any applicable statistical or foreign-investment filings. Do not treat an ordinary shareholder loan as equity; document and account for it separately.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Pay genuine supplier invoices by SEPA Credit Transfer for eligible euro-area payments or by SWIFT cross-border transfer, commonly MT103 or its ISO 20022 equivalent pacs.008 where supported. Match each payment to the contract, invoice, beneficiary account, and accounting record; specify charges and payment currency in the contract. For larger or documentary trade transactions, use a commercial letter of credit, documentary collection, or bank guarantee where commercially justified, with terms governed by the agreed rules such as UCP 600 for documentary credits. Retain customs and shipping documents when relevant. Apply withholding, VAT, transfer-pricing, sanctions, and deductibility checks before payment. Reconcile FX conversion rates, fees, settlement dates, and intercompany balances.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX forwards with a bank or authorized investment firm, supported by a documented underlying exposure and appropriate counterparty, suitability, and collateral arrangements.
Non-deliverable forwards where commercially relevant and legally available for the currencies and counterparties involved; settlement and regulatory treatment must be confirmed with the provider.
Currency swaps, including cross-currency swaps, subject to documented exposure, counterparty approval, valuation, collateral, and applicable EU derivatives rules.
FX options, where offered and appropriately assessed, with documented treasury authorization and understanding of premium, payoff, and potential loss.

Apply relevant MiFID II conduct and classification requirements, EMIR reporting, clearing, risk-mitigation, and collateral obligations as applicable to the counterparties and transaction. Use ISDA or equivalent documentation where appropriate; maintain an approved hedging policy and avoid speculative positions.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual approval of accounts and allocation of profit or loss by shareholders
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Company shareholders; minutes retained in the company's records
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within six months after the financial year-end, unless an extension is granted by the competent court
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to approve accounts may result in court-ordered compliance and director liability; no automatic strike-off

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Deposit of annual accounts and related documents
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Commercial Court Registry (Greffe du tribunal de commerce), for registration and publication through the commercial register
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within one month after approval; two months if filed electronically
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure may result in a court injunction, periodic penalty payments, and a fine generally up to EUR 1,500, increased for repeat offences; no automatic strike-off

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual corporate income tax return (Form 2065 and required schedules)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: French tax administration (Direction générale des Finances publiques)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within three months after financial year-end, or by the second business day following 1 May for a calendar-year accounting period
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing generally triggers a 10% surcharge, increased in specified circumstances, plus late-payment interest; persistent non-compliance may lead to tax enforcement, not automatic strike-off

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Update of beneficial-owner information, if reportable information changes
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Commercial Court Registry through the single window for business formalities
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 30 days after a change to reportable beneficial-owner information; no annual confirmation filing is generally required
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to file or maintain accurate information may result in criminal fines and other sanctions; no automatic strike-off

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: A statutory auditor is generally required when the SAS exceeds at least two of these thresholds at year-end: EUR 5 million total balance sheet, EUR 10 million net turnover, and 50 employees on average. Separate requirements may apply to groups, controlled entities, or regulated activities.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: French generally accepted accounting principles under the French Commercial Code and ANC regulations. IFRS is generally relevant to consolidated accounts of listed groups, not ordinary standalone SAS accounts.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: No general annual beneficial-owner confirmation is required. File an update with the commercial register within 30 days after a change in reportable information. Maintain current shareholder and corporate records.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of shareholders or movements in shares, maintained by the SAS
Register or records of decisions of shareholders
Minutes and decisions of the president and any other corporate bodies, as applicable

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: Approximately USD 300–1,200 annually, depending on provider and services
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: Approximately USD 3,000–10,000 annually for a small SAS subject to statutory audit; not applicable where no auditor is required

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 25% (plus 3.3% social surcharge on the portion of corporate income tax exceeding EUR 763,000, producing an effective marginal rate of 25.825% for large taxpayers)
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Reduced 15% rate on the first EUR 42,000 of taxable income for SMEs with turnover under EUR 10 million and qualifying shareholding; Research Tax Credit (CIR) at 30% of eligible R&D expenditure up to EUR 100 million; Innovation Tax Credit (CII) at 20%; Young Innovative Company (JEI) social and income tax exemptions; patent box regime at 10% for qualifying intellectual property income.
corporate_income_tax_regime.tax_loss_carryforward_limit_years: Unlimited in time (carryforward without statutory expiry), subject to an annual cap of EUR 1,000,000 plus 50% of the taxable profit exceeding EUR 1,000,000; carryback limited to EUR 1,000,000 for one year.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Form No. 2065-SD (liasse fiscale) with annexes 2050 to 2059; mandatory electronic filing through EFI/GEDI on impots.gouv.fr for all French companies.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual, for each fiscal year; separate instalment payments are made quarterly (monthly for large companies).
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Within three months of the fiscal year-end; for calendar-year companies the electronic filing deadline is 3 May of the following year (extended to 15 May for paper filers where allowed).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: SIREN, NAF/APE code, corporate form, registered office, and tax representative details.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Identify the French SAS as the taxable entity; if managed from abroad, ensure that the registered office and decision-making centres are properly disclosed to avoid creating a permanent establishment or a fictitious French seat.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net accounting income before tax, determined under French GAAP and before adjustments for tax purposes.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Reconcile foreign GAAP to French GAAP; add back non-deductible expenses and exclude exempt income; implement transfer pricing adjustments for intra-group service fees and software development charges.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax loss carryforward and carryback relief applied against the taxable result.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply the unlimited carryforward within the annual cap; maintain a legal loss ledger for audit by the French tax administration; non-resident shareholders cannot use the losses directly.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Computation of corporate tax at the reduced and standard rates, including eligible credits and prepayments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply the 25% standard rate, or 15% for qualifying SME profit within the EUR 42,000 band; recognise the CIR/CII only for activities carried on in France; settle quarterly instalments under the 2025 electronic payment regime.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing surcharge of 10% of the net tax due if filed after the deadline; 40% if filed after formal notice within 30 days; 80% for fraudulent obstruction. Late payment interest applies at 0.20% per month (2.4% annualised). Minimum penalties for non-electronic filing and failure to file tax annexes may also apply, plus director joint liability for management-created tax debts.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 30% final withholding tax on French-source dividends paid to non-resident corporate beneficiaries; 12.8% for non-resident individual shareholders plus applicable social levies; 0% for an EU/EEA corporate shareholder holding at least 10% for an uninterrupted 24-month period under the EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: The paying French SAS applies the reduced treaty rate at source only if the beneficiary submits a valid French tax residence certificate (Formulaire No. 5000/5001) before payment, together with an explicit beneficial-ownership declaration and entity substance documentation. If relief is not granted at source, the non-resident must file a refund claim with the French tax authorities (Service des impôts des particuliers / Direction des résidents à l'étranger) within the statutory limitation period, usually by 31 December of the second year following the dividend distribution. The treaty rate typically ranges from 0% to 15% depending on shareholding and the applicable Double Tax Agreement.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Royalties: domestic withholding tax of 33.33% under CGI Article 182 B for non-resident licensors; 0% under the EU Interest & Royalties Directive for qualifying EU associated companies; treaty rates commonly 0% to 10%. Interest: no general domestic withholding tax on arm's-length commercial interest paid to non-resident corporate lenders; 75% withholding applies to payments to non-cooperative jurisdictions; treaty rates commonly 0% to 10%.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Mandatory contemporaneous Master File and Local File for a French entity when its annual turnover or gross book assets exceed EUR 400 million or when it belongs to a group with such an entity; Country-by-Country report required for consolidated group revenue equal to or above EUR 750 million. Below these thresholds, the French tax administration may still require transfer pricing documentation during an audit, and the taxpayer should maintain a conceptual defence file.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: France does not apply the offshore Economic Substance Regulations model; instead, substance is tested through the doctrine of abuse of law (CGI Article L.64 LPF, now misused-legal-artifice doctrine), the requirement of beneficial ownership for treaty and EU Directive relief, and the permanent establishment / management-seat rules in CGI Article 209 and the OECD Model. A captive offshore development centre that invoicing re-characterizes as a French permanent establishment will be assessed untaxed profits plus a 40% bad-faith or 80% abuse-of-law penalty without sufficient personnel, functions, assets, and decision-making authority.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Willful omission of taxable profit, false invoicing, use of tax-haven shell companies, hiding a French permanent establishment under an ODC label, or presenting fabricated service agreements to shift profits outside France.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under CGI Article 1741 and Penal Code articles 1741 et seq., individuals face a fine of up to EUR 500,000 and five years' imprisonment; in aggravated cases, EUR 1,000,000 and ten years' imprisonment. A corporate defendant faces a fine equal to five times the individual fine (up to EUR 2,500,000 or EUR 5,000,000 aggravated). The tax administration adds a 40% to 80% civil majoration, 0.20% monthly interest, confiscation of unlawfully transferred assets, and publication of the judgment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who personally participated in the fraud are criminally liable and may be ordered to pay civil restitution to the French Treasury. The tax administration may pierce the corporate veil under CGI Article L.267 LPF, making directors jointly and severally liable for the company's tax debts where a serious managerial fault caused non-payment. Travel bans within the Schengen area, asset freezes, disqualification from corporate office, and extradition requests are enforceable against non-resident directors.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Creating and maintaining a French SAS without real employees, business premises, bank substance, economic risk, or coherent functional profile solely to access treaty benefits, derivative withholding exemptions, or to circulate invoices for offshore software development.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Recharacterization under the abuse-of-law procedure with an 80% penalty; denial of treaty or Directive benefits; retroactive tax reassessment with interest; DAC6 disclosures for transactions with hybrid mismatches or low-tax jurisdictions; possible dissolution order or tax reassessment of the parent company for unpaid French corporate tax.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Shareholders and managers can be held personally liable for the re-characterized tax debt where the shell's misuse constitutes a misuse of corporate assets (abus de biens sociaux). Criminal penalties include up to five years' imprisonment and EUR 375,000 fine; directors may be banned from managing a French or EU-domiciled business for up to 15 years and are subject to non-merger of personal and corporate patrimony where sham doctrine applies.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using the ODC as an invoice-clearing platform for money laundering, receiving third-party funds without KYC/CDD, concealing the beneficial owner, or executing transactions through Wise, Payoneer, or wire transfers while deliberately structuring payments to avoid French and EU reporting thresholds.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Articles 324-1 et seq. of the French Penal Code punish money laundering with five years' imprisonment and a EUR 375,000 fine for individuals; aggravated laundering attracts ten years and EUR 750,000, with corporate fines equal to five times the individual fine (up to EUR 3,750,000 or EUR 5,250,000 in aggravated cases). Breach of French Monetary and Financial Code obligations exposes additional administrative fines, Tracfin reporting sanctions, and preventive freezing orders.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are criminally liable for laundering operations they control or profit from. They may be subject to travel bans, international asset forfeiture, professional disqualification, and personal civil damages in favor of third-party victims. Corporate veil piercing is systematic in laundering cases where the SAS is used as a mere instrumentality, and D&O insurance cover is void for intentional AML offences.
